extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, analytic metaphysicians, and mathematically-informed philosophers or mathematicians interested in conceptual foundations and methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and pragmatic tests for when a mathematical definition, concept, or classification counts as 'objectively' natural or fruitful; focuses on how such judgments are supported by mathematical practice (conjecture, verification, generalization, explanatory role).

rubrics_metrics.name: Underwriting the intuitive natural/artificial distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: A recognized class of properties or categories should underwrite the intuitive distinction between natural and artificial cases in clear examples (Lewis’s item 1: 'Underwriting the intuitive natural/artificial distinction in clear cases').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple common-sense cases as prima facie tests (e.g. 'plus' vs 'quus'); but beware that some mathematical cases require expert training to appreciate. The paper treats this as one of the kinds of work a recognition of distinguished properties should do.

rubrics_metrics.name: Founding judgements of simplicity and similarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of distinguished properties should found judgements of simplicity and similarity, which inform theoretical constructions such as the selection of referents of variables for Ramsey sentences (Lewis’s item 2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations of simplicity and similarity are treated as theoretical virtues that influence conceptual choice; their role should be made explicit when arguing that a classification is natural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating general truths as lawlike or not
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguished properties should support evaluations of general truths as lawlike or not (Lewis’s item 3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a proposed classification helps explain why certain generalizations count as laws (or not) within the mathematical context at issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supporting assignments of content (Kripkenstein cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: The classification should support determinate assignments of content in underdetermined cases (for example in 'Kripkenstein' worries about meaning; Lewis’s item 4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the proposed concept pins down intended meanings/interpretations in cases where behavioural data alone underdetermines reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Underwriting intrinsic vs non-intrinsic distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinguished properties should underwrite a distinction between intrinsic and non-intrinsic properties (Lewis’s item 5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the proposed notion yields a principled partition of properties into intrinsic and non-intrinsic in ways that matter for mathematical practice or ontology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Singling out intended interpretations in cases of underdeterminacy
rubrics_metrics.description: A good classification should single out 'intended' interpretations where there is underdeterminacy (e.g. Löwenheim–Skolem type indeterminacy; Lewis’s item 6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the notion explains how mathematicians settle on intended models or interpretations despite formal underdetermination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing correct from incorrect inductive predictions ('grue' type examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: A notion of naturalness should help distinguish correct from incorrect inductive predictions in 'grue'-style problems (Lewis’s item 7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test whether the proposed category is 'projectible' in Goodman’s sense—i.e., whether it licenses successful inductive generalizations rather than arbitrary reclassifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity via confirmable consequences independent of the conjecture
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie sign that a judgement is objective is that it has consequences that can be confirmed or refuted and whose truth or falsehood is independent of the original conjecture (10.3: 'it is a prima facie sign that a judgement is objective if it has consequences that can be confirmed or refuted and whose truth or falsehood is independent of the original conjecture').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as a practical foothold: show the classification generates testable consequences (mathematical or quasi-empirical) that are not under the classifier’s control. Example: Euler’s conjectural reasoning about quadratic reciprocity produced predictions later verified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projectibility / inductive support
rubrics_metrics.description: Categories count as natural to the extent that they support successful inductive reasoning and projectible generalizations (Goodman/Euler analogy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the classification allows the mathematician to make predictions about further cases that are borne out on further inspection; the mathematical analogue of 'green' vs 'grue' is used to illustrate this test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fruitfulness and significance (quasi-empirical inductive character)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological virtues like 'significance' and 'fruitfulness' have a quasi-empirical inductive character: singling out a property as central tacitly predicts it will reappear in unexpected contexts and generate new mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether adopting the concept leads to novel discoveries or unexpected appearances in different parts of theory; fruitfulness is taken as evidence for objective naturalness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding problem-solving and discovery (potential for discovering proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good definition or concept should improve the potential for discovering proofs and guide problem-solving (improved understanding, enhanced potential for discovering proofs, 'purity of method').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the notion streamlines reasoning, suggests strategies, or leads to more direct or purer proofs; see 'purity of method' considerations and Detlefsen’s contribution cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory power and provision of understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: A notion counts in its favour if it provides explanatory connections and conceptual stepping stones (e.g. proofs of quadratic reciprocity via cyclotomic extensions leading to Artin reciprocity; Legendre symbol becoming a special case of Artin symbol).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for cases where the concept clarifies why disparate results cohere, or where it situates an object as a special case of a deeper, more general concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity of method and other theoretical virtues (simplicity, elegance, loveliness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals to theoretical virtues such as simplicity, elegance, and 'purity of method' are standard grounds for preferring one account over another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper warns these appeals are context-sensitive and need justification if they are to count as objective (see discussion of why theoretical virtues might or might not track ontology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-pragmatic mathematical reasons vs 'mere mathematical convenience'
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all reasons for preferring a representation are merely pragmatic bookkeeping conveniences—some mathematical reasons (e.g. generalizability, explanatory payoff) can be substantive grounds for preferring one representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: von Neumann ordinals are preferred over Zermelo because the von Neumann generating principle generalizes to infinite ordinals; resist collapsing all such reasons into 'merely pragmatic'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance to gerrymandered or artificial definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions or reductions that are grotesquely gerrymandered or artificially contrived count against naturalness; natural notions should exclude such pathological constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use constructed pathological examples as negative controls: if a proposed criterion would count obviously gerrymandered constructions as natural, it is inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generativity / generalizability across contexts (finite → infinite, local → global)
rubrics_metrics.description: A representation or principle that generalizes naturally beyond special cases (e.g. from finite ordinals to infinite ordinals) is a mark of naturalness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the principle generating a structure extends uniformly to broader domains without ad hoc patches (von Neumann example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Testability through computation and inductive refinement (conjecture → test → refine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical practice often uses computational records, conjecture based on examined cases, and subsequent verification/refutation to refine concepts; the ability to enter this cycle is evidence of naturalness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Euler’s use of computations, conjecture of quadratic reciprocity, and subsequent verification are paradigmatic; prefer concepts that enable this productive cycle rather than ones that block it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context-sensitivity and the limits of intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: Intuitions about objectivity and naturalness are extremely context-sensitive; offhand appeals to simplicity or aesthetic plausibility may be misleading when detached from mathematical practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat intuitive judgments as provisional; where possible, supplement with concrete demonstrations of fruitfulness, generalizability, testable consequences, or other harder criteria. The paper stresses the need for 'harder criteria of objectivity' beyond intuition.
